title: Ransomware Intrusion at a Regional Water Utility
confidence_notes: Attribution and dwell-time figures are drawn from the internal report and not independently verified.
headline: Corporate ransomware forced protective shutdowns but did not affect water supply
key_points: An attacker used a contractor credential without multi-factor authentication to reach the corporate network.
File-encrypting malware hit eleven servers, including billing and the historian database.
Operational technology controlling treatment and distribution was segmented and unaffected.
Offline backups at a separate site made recovery possible after online backups were deleted.
Billing was restored in four days; historian data took nine days.
context: The utility detected anomalous outbound traffic at 02:40 and contained the intrusion within ninety minutes, but encryption had already spread across core corporate systems.
implications: A purely corporate compromise can still degrade public service by forcing network decoupling.
Unrotated third-party credentials remain the highest-value target for intrusion.
Backup isolation is now a board-level resilience question, not only an IT control.
recommended_actions: Rotate every contractor credential and enforce multi-factor authentication on all remote access.
Isolate backup infrastructure so domain administrator accounts cannot reach it.
Deploy endpoint detection and response to all servers and engineering workstations.
Run a tabletop exercise on decoupling corporate and operational networks under time pressure.
one_line_takeaway: Segmentation saved the water supply; weak contractor identity hygiene nearly lost the business.
